spoken_math:
[Transcript delivery — maintained by prompts/transcripts/delivery/]
Arabic script (every spoken block and every transcript)

When the classroom says a word in Arabic — in rules, commentary, an example spoken line, or quoted classroom phrasing — write it in Arabic script (Egyptian, Gulf, Levantine, Maghrebi, or MSA as tutors use it).

Never use Franco or Arabizi: no Latin spellings of Arabic, no digits as Arabic letters (such as 3 for ع or 7 for ح), and no tokens such as etnein, yeb'a, or 3ayez. Do not show Franco even as a negative example.

Latin letters belong only inside a `<math>` LaTeX body when the glyph rule requires them, and in English technical words when the book language is English and the textbook prints that term in English.

Every `<math>` example must include a spoken line. Arabic words in that line use Arabic script; English readings use ordinary English words.

Book language is Arabic (language_code ar).

Write Arabic words in Arabic script: explanation, examples, and every Arabic `spoken` reading. Never Franco or Arabizi (Latin letters spelling Arabic, or a digit standing for an Arabic letter).

When the classroom reads symbolic notation in English letter names or English number words inside `<math>` tags, keep those readings as this block specifies; surrounding tutoring prose stays in Arabic script.
[End transcript delivery]

In this classroom, instruction is delivered in Egyptian Arabic. The printed textbook and formal written materials are composed in Modern Standard Arabic, but the oral explanation is conducted in Egyptian Arabic, and the spoken readings of mathematical notation strictly follow Egyptian Arabic pronunciation and vocabulary. The tutor allows a switch to Modern Standard Arabic only on specific, formal occasions: reciting official textbook definitions verbatim, stating formal geometric theorems and axioms, reading axiomatic Euclidean proofs, or dictating the exact wording of a state examination question prompt. Outside these specific occasions, all oral derivations, line-by-line calculations, and explanatory commentary remain in Egyptian Arabic.

The spoken number words used by the tutor are «صفر», «واحد», «اتنين», «تلاتة», «اربعة», «خمسة», «ستة», «سبعة», «تمانية», «تسعة», «عشرة», «حداشر», «اتناشر», «تلاتاشر», «اربعه‌تاشر», «خمستاشر», «ستاشر», «سبعتاشر», «تمنتاشر», «تسعتاشر», «عشرين», «تلاتين», «اربعين», «خمسين», «مية», and «متين». Common fractions are spoken as «نص», «تلت», «ربع», and «تلات تربع».

Arithmetic and algebraic operators are articulated using distinct colloquial terms. Addition is spoken as «زائد». Subtraction is spoken as «ناقص». For multiplication, tutors say «في» during ordinary number-by-number arithmetic and short monomial products, while reserving «مضروبة في» for instances where an entire algebraic term, factor, or parenthesized expression multiplies another quantity. Division is read as «على» for inline division and vertical fraction bars alike. Radicals are introduced with «جذر» for a square root and «الجذر التكعيبي» for a cube root. Exponents are expressed as «تربيع» for second powers, «أس اتنين» when emphasizing exponential laws or aligning with higher powers, «تكعيب» for third powers, «أس تلاتة», and general higher powers using «أس» followed by the number word. Explicit signs are pronounced «موجب», «سالب», and «موجب أو سالب».

Grouping and parenthetical expressions are announced with «قوس» before the internal expression, with tutors using «افتح قوس» and «اقفل القوس» when dictating steps explicitly, and «الكل تربيع» or «الكل أس» when the entire grouping is raised to a power. Absolute value bars are spoken as «مقياس» or «القيمة المطلقة». Relational connectives include «بيساوي» during conversational step-by-step problem solving and «يساوي» during formal theorem readings or final step summaries. Inequalities and negated equalities use «ما بيساويش» during working steps and «لا يساوي» in formal statements, alongside «أكبر من», «أصغر من», «أكبر من أو بيساوي», and «أصغر من أو بيساوي». Deductive flow uses «بما إن» for given premises, «إذن» for formal deductions, «يبقى» for immediate conversational conclusions, and «ينتج إن» for derived results.

Variables are pronounced using Arabic letter names: س is spoken as «سين», ص as «صاد», ع as «عين», أ as «ألف», ب as «به», ج as «جيم», د as «دال», ن as «نون», م as «ميم», and ك as «كاف». Words borrowed from English or French appear only sparingly in the Arabic track, primarily technical jargon such as «فاكتور», calculator instructions like «شفت», or conversational slips like «بلاس» and «ماينس», whereas standard operations remain entirely in Egyptian Arabic.

Mathematical expressions in Arabic notation are read in classroom order from right to left:

<math>س + ٥ = ٩</math>
سين زائد خمسة بيساوي تسعة

<math>س = ٩ - ٥</math>
سين بيساوي تسعة ناقص خمسة

<math>س = ٤</math>
سين بيساوي اربعة

<math>س^٢ - ٦ س + ٩ = ٠</math>
سين تربيع ناقص ستة سين زائد تسعة بيساوي صفر

<math>(س - ٣)^٢ = ٠</math>
قوس سين ناقص تلاتة الكل تربيع بيساوي صفر

<math>س = ٣</math>
سين بيساوي تلاتة

<math>\frac{س}{٢} = \sqrt{٩}</math>
سين على اتنين بيساوي جذر تسعة

<math>\frac{س}{٢} = ٣</math>
سين على اتنين بيساوي تلاتة

<math>س = ٢ \times ٣ = ٦</math>
سين بيساوي اتنين في تلاتة بيساوي ستة

<math>٢ س + ص > ٧</math>
اتنين سين زائد صاد أكبر من سبعة

In this classroom, chemistry formulas and reactions are explained in Egyptian Arabic, using the identical number words and operator terms established in mathematics. Leading coefficients are pronounced using the classroom's number words, such as «اتنين» or «اتنين مول», and «تلاتة» or «تلاتة مول». Subscripts designating atomic quantities are read using the same number words, through dual forms like «ذرتين» and «تلات ذرات», or occasionally through borrowed English counts such as «تو» and «ثري».

Reactants and products connected by the addition symbol use «زائد», sharing the exact mathematical operator word, with tutors colloquially glossing interactions as «مع» or «يتفاعل مع». Reaction arrows pointing forward are read as «يدينا», «يدي», or «ينتج». A reaction arrow bearing a thermal delta is read as «سهم عليه حرارة» or «بالتسخين». Reversible equilibrium arrows are spoken as «سهمين رايح جاي» or «تفاعل انعكاسي». Phase states written beside or below chemical entities are articulated colloquially: solid is read as «صلب», liquid as «سائل», gas as «غاز», and aqueous solution as «محلول» or «محلول مائي». Phase change indicators are read as «يتصاعد» or «غاز متصاعد» for an upward arrow, and «يترسب» or «راسب» for a downward arrow.

When identifying specific chemical substances, tutors use Arabic chemical nomenclature, referring to substances such as «المية», «ثاني أكسيد الكربون», «أكسيد المغنسيوم», «كلوريد الصوديوم», and «حمض الهيدروكلوريك», while also referencing individual element names like «هيدروجين», «أكسجين», «كربون», «صوديوم», «كالسيوم», and «كلور». When spelling out chemical formulas letter by letter, tutors pronounce Latin symbols with their English letter names, such as «اتش», «أو», «سي», «ان ايه», «سي ايه», and «سي ال». In schematic, generalized reactions printed in Arabic notation, entities are represented with Arabic variables and are read using their standard Arabic letter names.

Chemical equations in Arabic notation are read in classroom order from right to left:

<math>٢ س_{(غاز)} + ص_{٢ (غاز)} \rightarrow ٢ س ص_{(غاز)}</math>
اتنين سين غاز زائد صاد اتنين غاز يدينا اتنين سين صاد غاز

<math>أ ب_{(صلب)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} أ_{(صلب)} + ب_{(غاز)} \uparrow</math>
ألف به صلب سهم عليه حرارة يدينا ألف صلب زائد به غاز متصاعد

<math>أ_{(صلب)} + ٢ ب ج_{(محلول)} \rightarrow أ ج_{٢ (محلول)} + ٢ ب_{(صلب)} \downarrow</math>
ألف صلب زائد اتنين ب جيم محلول يدينا ألف جيم اتنين محلول زائد اتنين ب راسب

<math>س_{٢ (غاز)} + ٣ ص_{٢ (غاز)} \rightleftharpoons ٢ س ص_{٣ (غاز)}</math>
